lines: Thunder shook the stonecutter so hard loose stones rattled in the wall, but everyone near me is still standing.
I checked walls, steps, and cracked blocks after the lightning, then counted heads. No one should be alone after a sky like that.
Near the stonecutter, the bell sounded small under that thunder. We stayed inside and kept the doors watched.
That thunder made everyone quiet. I checked the doorframes twice.
The sky can keep its lightning. I have doorframes to set right.
I checked wooden beams set into stone for sparks first, then checked faces for smoke and <dark_gray><wavy>fear</wavy></dark_gray>.
We passed water hand to hand and kept people away from the smoke. I checked the stonecutter after.
The stonecutter can wait. People come first.
We saved what we could reach around the stonecutter, then stopped pretending things matter more than neighbors.
The smoke is thinning near the stonecutter, but everyone is still sniffing the air like it might lie.
During a raid, the stonecutter can sit silent. Who makes it behind a door matters more.
The horns stopped, but my hands near the stonecutter still expect another wave from the road.
We counted living neighbors before walls, steps, and cracked blocks. That's the only count worth starting with.
Raiders came looking for easy emeralds. They found barred doors near the stonecutter and a bell that would not stop ringing.
From the stonecutter, I saw fear cross the square. Then I saw courage get there first.
Night trouble tests the loose latch by the stonecutter first. We are fixing those before sunset.
I stayed near the wall with the missing block and listened for anyone calling from the dark.
Dawn gave the stonecutter enough light to count wounds, missing blocks, and who made it home.
The dark tested everyone. Most of us passed by keeping a stack of spare stone between us and teeth.
We are safe enough near the stonecutter, though every shadow is being inspected twice.
The wind threw sand through every crack. I am still cleaning sand from the mortar lines.
I checked walls, steps, and cracked blocks, then checked who was coughing too hard to answer.
Sand reached the stonecutter, the hinges, and half our eyes, but no one has been reported missing.
A hard wind teaches a mason which doors actually close and which ones only pretend.
We are safe enough near the stonecutter, though the whole village sounds like it is chewing gravel.
The stonecutter can sit silent. Warm hands, clear paths, and full hearths come first.
Snow piled against the doors, but everyone near the stonecutter found shelter.
Cold works quietly around the stonecutter. We are checking on anyone who stayed quiet too long.
I am clearing ice off the steps and watching for footprints that stop too soon.
We are alright for now near the stonecutter. Keep the fires fed and the paths open.
